questions.prompt:
The Euclidean algorithm allows one to find the greatest common divisor of two integers by repeatedly applying the fact that, if $a\le b$, $\gcd(a,b)=\gcd(b\bmod a,a)$, where $b\bmod a$ is the remainder after dividing $b$ by $a$. This algorithm continuously replaces $b$ with $b\bmod a$ until one of the numbers is zero. For example, we can find the gcd of $10$ and $12$ as follows: $\gcd(10,12)=\gcd(2,10)$ because $12\bmod10$ is $2$, which equals $\gcd(0,2)$ because $10\bmod2$ is $0$. The other term, $2$, is thus $\gcd(10,12)$.

Let $f(a,b)$ be the number of iterations in the Euclidean algorithm. For example, $f(10,12)=2$, $f(2,4)=1$, and $f(5,8)=4$. Find $f(1,2025)+f(2,2025)+\cdots+f(2025,2025)$.

(Estimation: submit a positive integer $E$; if the correct answer is $A$, the score is $\operatorname{round}\left(25\exp\left(-4.5\frac{|E-A|}{A}\right)\right)$.)
questions.answer: Official answer $12337$ (scored by closeness to this value).

questions.prompt: Prove that for any fraction $\frac pq>1$ there is a unique finite sequence of positive integers $a_1,\dots,a_n$ with $a_1>1$ such that $$\frac pq=a_n+\cfrac1{a_{n-1}+\cfrac1{\ddots+\cfrac1{a_2+\cfrac1{a_1}}}}.$$
questions.answer: Euclidean algorithm gives existence; the integer part forces uniqueness.

questions.prompt: A tangle diagram is a diagram in a disk with two strings whose four endpoints are at NW, NE, SE, SW. The integer tangle $[N]$ has $N$ horizontal crossings (alternating type, $[-N]=-[N]$ with all crossings switched); $\frac1P$ is $P$ rotated $90^\circ$ clockwise with all crossings switched; $P+Q$ places $P$ and $Q$ side by side and $P*Q$ stacks them vertically; $P\sim Q$ means they are related by Reidemeister moves keeping the endpoints fixed. Prove that for any rational tangles $P$ and $Q$, $$P-\frac1Q\sim P-[1]+\cfrac1{[1]+\cfrac1{Q-[1]}},$$ by demonstrating an appropriate sequence of diagrams and/or Reidemeister moves. (You may use that rational tangles are equivalent to their horizontal and vertical flips, and the Product-to-Inverse Equivalence.)
questions.answer: Reduce to a diagrammatic identity for a crossing next to $Q$, proved by R3, rotation and the flip $Q\sim Q^v$.
questions.reviewNote: The key move is a picture-level identity (R3 and rotation); the textual sketch here follows the official diagrams but cannot reproduce them in full.

questions.answer: Both reduce to the same canonical positive continued fraction tangle.

questions.prompt: Knots are closed loops of string; a knot diagram is a drawing recording which strand passes over or under at each crossing (no more than two strands cross at a point). A crossing change reverses which strand passes over the other at a single crossing. Name a set of crossings in the knot diagram shown (a trefoil with crossings labeled 1, 2, 3) that, when each is changed, results in a diagram equivalent to the unknot.
questions.answer: Any one or two of the three crossings.

questions.prompt: Knots are closed loops of string; a knot diagram is a drawing recording which strand passes over or under at each crossing (no more than two strands cross at a point). Which of the two knot diagrams shown (left or right) is equivalent to the unknot?

Knots are closed loops of string; a knot diagram is a drawing recording which strand passes over or under at each crossing (no more than two strands cross at a point). A crossing change reverses which strand passes over the other at a single crossing. Prove that in any knot diagram there is some set of crossing changes that makes the diagram equivalent to the unknot.
questions.answer: Make the knot monotonically descending, so it has no crossings when viewed from the side.

questions.prompt: Knots are closed loops of string; a knot diagram is a drawing recording which strand passes over or under at each crossing (no more than two strands cross at a point). A crossing change reverses which strand passes over the other at a single crossing. Prove that in any knot diagram with $N$ crossings, the minimum number of crossing changes needed to make the diagram equivalent to the unknot is at most $N/2$.
questions.answer: If $k>N/2$ changes work, change the other $N-k<N/2$ crossings instead (mirror image).

questions.prompt: Knots are closed loops of string; a knot diagram is a drawing recording which strand passes over or under at each crossing (no more than two strands cross at a point). A crossing change reverses which strand passes over the other at a single crossing. A region crossing change (RCC) on a region performs a crossing change on every crossing on the boundary of that region (the region outside the knot counts as a region). Suppose $R$ and $S$ are regions of a knot diagram. Prove that performing an RCC on $R$ followed by an RCC on $S$ gives the same diagram as performing an RCC on $S$ followed by an RCC on $R$.
questions.answer: Each crossing ends up changed iff it was changed an odd number of times.

questions.prompt: A crossing is reducible if some region is adjacent to it twice (two of its four corners belong to the same region); a diagram is reduced if none of its crossings is reducible. Suppose the crossing shown in the figure (with the four surrounding regions $A,B,C,D$ in order around the crossing) is from an arbitrary knot diagram. Which regions other than $A$ could be the same region as $A$?

Knots are closed loops of string; a knot diagram is a drawing recording which strand passes over or under at each crossing (no more than two strands cross at a point). The Reidemeister moves are: R1 (twist or untwist a loop, adding or removing one crossing), R2 (slide one strand over or under another, adding or removing two crossings), and R3 (slide a strand across a crossing, keeping the number of crossings); by Reidemeister's theorem two diagrams show the same knot exactly when they are related by a sequence of these moves. A checkerboard coloring of a knot diagram shades some regions so that regions sharing an edge segment have opposite shades (regions meeting only at a crossing are not adjacent); the outside region counts. Prove that checkerboard colorability is unchanged by Reidemeister moves: if a Reidemeister move is performed on a checkerboard colorable diagram, the new diagram can still be checkerboard colored. (You may not use the fact that every knot diagram is checkerboard colorable.)
questions.answer: Keep all colors outside the small disk of the move and color the new inner regions consistently.

A crossing change reverses which strand passes over the other at a single crossing. Prove that every knot diagram can be checkerboard colored. (You may use that checkerboard colorability is unchanged by Reidemeister moves, and that any diagram can be changed into a diagram of the unknot by crossing changes.)
questions.answer: The coloring does not depend on which strand is over; reduce to a diagram of the unknot, which is obtained from the circle by Reidemeister moves.

questions.prompt: A region crossing change (RCC) on a region performs a crossing change on every crossing on the boundary of that region (the region outside the knot counts as a region). A crossing is reducible if some region is adjacent to it twice (two of its four corners belong to the same region); a diagram is reduced if none of its crossings is reducible. A checkerboard coloring of a knot diagram shades some regions so that regions sharing an edge segment have opposite shades (regions meeting only at a crossing are not adjacent); the outside region counts. Consider a reduced knot diagram with a checkerboard coloring. Prove that performing RCC moves on all shaded regions leaves the original diagram unchanged.
questions.answer: Each crossing is surrounded by exactly two distinct shaded regions.

questions.prompt: A link is a collection of closed loops (components). A splice at a crossing $c$ of an oriented knot diagram removes the crossing by reconnecting the strands so as to respect the orientation (the region where $c$ was becomes a single region $R$). Prove that a splice on a knot diagram always converts it into a link diagram with exactly two components.
questions.answer: The part of the knot between the two visits to $c$ closes up into one loop and the rest into the other.

A link is a collection of closed loops (components). A splice at a crossing $c$ of an oriented knot diagram removes the crossing by reconnecting the strands so as to respect the orientation (the region where $c$ was becomes a single region $R$). The three-step operation on a crossing $c$ of a knot diagram: (1) splice $c$, and let $R$ be the region formed at the splice; (2) in the resulting link diagram, checkerboard color one of the two components $A$ (ignoring the other component $B$) choosing the coloring in which $R$ is unshaded; (3) undo the splice, remember which regions were shaded, and perform an RCC on every shaded region of the unspliced diagram. Prove that the three-step operation on a crossing $c$ is equivalent to a crossing change on $c$ alone, if every crossing other than $c$ is not reducible.
questions.answer: Count shaded regions around each crossing: exactly one at $c$, and an even number of distinct ones at every other crossing.

questions.answer: Do the three-step operation on $c$, and if $d$ was flipped, do the three-step operation on $d$.

questions.answer: A closed curve through the splice region separates the two components.

questions.prompt: A link is a collection of closed loops (components). A crossing is reducible if some region is adjacent to it twice (two of its four corners belong to the same region); a diagram is reduced if none of its crossings is reducible. (You may use Question 4.13.)
questions.answer: Splice at a reducible crossing, and move the splice to a reducible crossing on the component not containing $c$ until the other component is reduced.

A splice at a crossing $c$ of an oriented knot diagram removes the crossing by reconnecting the strands so as to respect the orientation (the region where $c$ was becomes a single region $R$). The three-step operation on a crossing $c$ of a knot diagram: (1) splice $c$, and let $R$ be the region formed at the splice; (2) in the resulting link diagram, checkerboard color one of the two components $A$ (ignoring the other component $B$) choosing the coloring in which $R$ is unshaded; (3) undo the splice, remember which regions were shaded, and perform an RCC on every shaded region of the unspliced diagram.
